title: Cooper Desmond
text:
Research Professional, University of Chicago Booth School of Business
I study how institutions (e.g., courts, clinics, schools) shape people’s health, mobility, and civic lives. My methodological focus is using quasi-experimental designs to make causal arguments that inform policy-relevant questions. These designs usually require linking data across several institutions, so I often work with partner organizations (e.g., community health centers, legal clinics, county agencies) to build multi-institutional datasets that serve our research goals. This has led to my second methodological interest in scaling and refining probabilistic record linkage models, since the quality of the linkage can affect the resulting estimates.

title: Cooper Desmond
text:
Policy Research

Working papers

Felony Conviction, Voting, and Recidivism: Evidence from Harris County
Working paper
In Texas, a felony conviction removes a person from the voter rolls until their sentence is fully discharged, after which they must re-register on their own. Using the random assignment of felony cases to courts in Harris County, this paper estimates the effect of a felony conviction on voter registration and recidivism, adding civic participation to the recidivism and labor-market outcomes that leniency designs usually study. Because disenfranchisement follows any felony conviction rather than a particular disposition, the instrument is coarsened to each court’s felony conviction rate, collapsing prison, jail, probation, misdemeanor, deferral, and dismissal into convicted and not convicted. Building on Humphries et al. (2025), the paper shows that the resulting estimate equals the effect of conviction for cases whose conviction status the court changes, plus bias from cases a stricter court resolves differently without changing whether they are convicted, and develops interpretations of the bias.

The association of patient and disease characteristics with the overtreatment of low-risk prostate cancer from 2010 to 2016 (DOI)
Cooper Desmond, Sumedh Kaul, Aaron Fleishman, Ruslan Korets, Peter Chang, Andrew Wagner, Simon P. Kim, Nima Aghdam, Aria F. Olumi, Boris Gershman
Prostate Cancer and Prostatic Diseases, 2024
Although active surveillance is the preferred management for low-risk prostate cancer (PCa), some men remain at risk of overtreatment with definitive local therapy. We hypothesized that baseline characteristics may be associated with overtreatment and represent a potential source of health disparities. We therefore examined the associations of patient and disease characteristics with the surgical overtreatment of low-risk PCa. We identified men aged 45–75 years with cT1 cN0 cM0 prostate adenocarcinoma with biopsy Gleason score 6 and PSA < 10 ng/ml from 2010–2016 in the National Cancer Database (NCDB) and who underwent radical prostatectomy (RP). We evaluated the associations of baseline characteristics with clinically insignificant PCa (iPCa) at RP (i.e., “overtreatment”), defined as organ-confined (i.e., pT2) Gleason 3 + 3 disease, using multivariable logistic regression. We observed an ~27% reduction in rates of overtreatment of men with low-risk PCa over the study period. Several patient, disease, and structural characteristics are associated with detection of iPCa at RP and can inform the management of men with low-risk PCa to reduce potential overtreatment.

Evaluation
I’ve led evaluations for health centers and nonprofits, ranging from mixed-methods program reviews to quasi-experimental impact studies built on linked administrative data.

Disability Insurance, Legal Aid, and Prenatal Care: Evidence from a Farmworker Health Center
In progress
Evaluates whether the clinic’s medical-legal partnership and California State Disability Insurance enrollment improve prenatal care access and birth outcomes among farmworker patients, using linked health and disability-benefits records with synthetic and within-clinic controls.


Shared Success Midpoint Evaluation Overview (Link)
Cooper Desmond, Barbara Magnoni
Aspen Institute, 2025, with EA Consultants and the NYU Financial Access Initiative
Mixed-methods evaluation of Shared Success, an Aspen Institute Economic Opportunities Program demonstration in which 11 community development financial institutions (CDFIs) across the United States built job-quality advising into the support they give small-business owners. Working with the Financial Access Initiative and EA Consultants, I led the evaluation’s quantitative and qualitative data collection and analysis. At the midpoint, surveys and interviews with participating business owners documented which job-quality changes they had made, why they made them, what stood in the way, and what they planned next. At endline, the evaluation returned to the owners and added surveys and interviews with their workers.

title: Cooper Desmond
text:
Methods

Selection on Observables as an IV Thought Experiment (PDF)
Cooper Desmond
Note, 2026
This note frames selection on observables as an instrumental variables design by letting the regressor of interest serve as its own instrument, so that once the controls are partialled out the instrument is the residual variation in the treatment. With homogeneous effects, it shows by Frisch-Waugh-Lovell that OLS with controls and just-identified IV are the same estimator, and that instrument validity is exactly the no omitted variable bias condition. Relevance turns out to be the OLS full rank condition, and exclusion holds trivially. The note also shows that the homoskedastic asymptotic variances coincide. The variance inflation factor is therefore the inverse of a first-stage R-squared, and multicollinearity is a weak first stage for the instrument OLS uses implicitly. What separates the two designs is the source of the identifying variation and how it can be defended, since OLS has to treat all of the variation left after the controls as good as random while IV makes that claim only for the variation an external instrument induces. The note concludes that controls define the instrument rather than identify the effect, and it suggests reading every regression with controls as a just-identified IV regression and asking it the questions one would ask of an instrument.


Theory Behind Splink: The Fellegi-Sunter Model and EM, Estimation in Splink, and Extensions (PDF, Repo)
Cooper Desmond
Note, 2026
A walkthrough of how Splink estimates and applies the Fellegi-Sunter model of probabilistic record linkage. It first derives the model from the conditional independence assumption, including the posterior match probability, the match weight, and the expectation-maximization (EM) updates, with a proof that an EM update cannot decrease the likelihood. It then describes how Splink departs from textbook EM by estimating the prior from deterministic rules, estimating the non-match parameters from random sampling, running EM within blocks, and adjusting for term frequency. The final section presents three extensions to the Splink workflow, which are a sampling scheme for EM training when the data contain multiple ranked observations of entities that gives every row the same inclusion probability (while keeping at most one row per individual), parallel prediction over shards of the data, and one-to-one link enforcement through mutual best links or a linear sum assignment.
